job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

response.passage: In our history workshop today, we examined the complex causes behind the 1857 uprising. We learned that while the greased cartridges served as the immediate spark, the revolt was fueled by deep-seated grievances across all levels of society. Peasants, burdened by heavy taxes and oppressive revenue collection, were just as resentful as the sepoys. We also analyzed the Doctrine of Lapse, which the British used specifically to annex kingdoms lacking a natural male heir, rather than seizing any territory at will. Furthermore, we discussed how the British government, fearing future uprisings, reorganized the army by reducing the proportion of Indian soldiers to ensure tighter control. Finally, we clarified that the British East India Company’s rule officially ended in 1858, when the British Crown took direct control of India through the Government of India Act. This shift marked a fundamental change in how the subcontinent was governed, ending the era of Company rule long before the twentieth century. By looking at these diverse factors, we see that the revolt was not a single-issue event but a massive reaction to decades of colonial policies that affected every Indian, from the rural farmer to the royal families whose lands were taken away.
response.summary: The 1857 revolt was caused by a combination of economic, political, and military grievances rather than a single event. After the uprising, the British government took direct control of India from the East India Company.
